original_value: To recommend the next item to a user in a transactional context is practical yet challenging in applications such as marketing campaigns. Transactional context refers to the items that are observable in a transaction. Most existing transaction based recommender systems (TBRSs) make recommendations by mainly considering recently occurring items instead of all the ones observed in the current context. Moreover, they often assume a rigid order between items within a transaction, which is not always practical. More importantly, a long transaction often contains many items irreverent to the next choice, which tends to overwhelm the influence of a few truly relevant ones. Therefore, we posit that a good TBRS should not only consider all the observed items in the current transaction but also weight them with different relevance to build an attentive context that outputs the proper next item with a high probability. To this end, we design an effective attention based transaction embedding model (ATEM) for context embedding to weight each observed item in a transaction without assuming order. The empirical study on real-world transaction datasets proves that ATEM significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art methods in terms of both accuracy and novelty.

result.paraphrase: Recommending the next item to a user in transactional settings is both useful and difficult, as in marketing campaigns. Here, transactional context means the items visible within a transaction. Most existing transaction-based recommender systems (TBRSs) base their predictions mainly on recently appearing items rather than all items observed in the current context. They also tend to assume a fixed order among transaction items, which is not always practical. More importantly, lengthy transactions often include many items irrelevant to the next choice, which can drown out the influence of a few truly relevant ones. We therefore argue that a strong TBRS should consider every observed item in the current transaction and assign each a different level of relevance, forming an attentive context that is more likely to produce the right next item. To do this, we develop an effective attention-based transaction embedding model (ATEM) for context embedding that weights each observed item in a transaction without assuming any order. Empirical evaluation on real-world transaction datasets shows that ATEM substantially surpasses state-of-the-art methods in both accuracy and novelty.
